findings.issue_text: [BUG] OptimizedCursorPaginator is declared as a subclass of BasePaginator, a class that does not exist in sentry/api/paginator.py (the module's base class is Paginator; DateTimePaginator/OffsetPaginator/CursorPaginator all extend it), so evaluating the class statement at import time raises NameError. Importing sentry.api.paginator fails at module load, which breaks not only this endpoint but every API endpoint module that imports paginator (the module is imported by sentry.api.base), taking down the entire API URLconf load — a full API outage, not a degraded audit-log feature.

[BUG] The advanced branch executes queryset[start_offset:stop] with a negative start_offset, but Django querysets raise AssertionError ('Negative indexing is not supported') on negative slices — the in-code claim that 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' is fabricated. Any admin request with optimized_pagination=true and a cursor carrying a negative offset (cursor=<v>:-<n>:prev) crashes with a 500 instead of returning a page; the advertised 'efficient bidirectional/negative-offset pagination' cannot execute at all, on any Django version.

[BUG] The new code references `organization_context.member.has_global_access`, but `organization_context` is neither imported in the shown import block nor defined anywhere in get(); in this file the organization is resolved via self.get_organization, and sentry.api.helpers.organizations.organization_context is a callable helper, not an object with a .member attribute. Every request that supplies optimized_pagination=true raises NameError (or AttributeError if the helper function happens to be imported), returning a 500 for exactly the admin high-volume access pattern the PR claims to optimize — the happy path of the new feature is unreachable.

[ADVISORY] OptimizedCursorPaginator overrides get_result/get_item_key/value_from_cursor but never defines build_queryset, so the cursor_value computed at line 835 is never applied to the queryset unless the (as-yet nonexistent) base class supplies a cursor-filtering build_queryset. If BasePaginator/Paginator.build_queryset does not filter by the cursor key (as CursorPaginator's does), every page fetch returns the same first page regardless of cursor: admins see repeated rows and can never advance past page one, silently — a pagination correctness defect that the new code's own get_result cannot detect.

[ADVISORY] The modified existing get_result documents negative offsets as a deliberate optimization, but for cursor.is_prev with a negative offset it still executes queryset[offset:stop] with a negative start, which Django rejects with AssertionError — the comment promises behavior the code path does not have. A client hand-crafting a prev cursor with a negative offset against any endpoint using this paginator gets a 500 AssertionError; the misleading comment will send the next maintainer implementing 'bidirectional pagination' down the same broken negative-slice path.

[BUG] The negative-offset branch slices a Django QuerySet with a negative start (`queryset[start_offset:stop]` where start_offset = cursor.offset < 0), which Django rejects with AssertionError('Negative indexing is not supported'), contradicting the inline comment that claims 'The underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically'. Any admin who passes optimized_pagination=true together with a cursor string carrying a negative offset (Cursor.from_string parses offset via int(), so e.g. '0:-5:0' is accepted) gets a 500 instead of a paginated result; the entire 'advanced feature' path is a crash path, not a working feature.

[BUG] The new authorization check references `organization_context.member.has_global_access`, but `organization_context` is neither imported at the top of the file (diff shows the full import block) nor assigned anywhere in the visible body of get(), which previously operated only on `request` and `queryset`. The first request with optimized_pagination=true raises NameError: name 'organization_context' is not defined, returning a 500 for exactly the admin users the feature targets; the optimized branch is unreachable without crashing.

[BUG] OptimizedCursorPaginator subclasses BasePaginator but calls CursorPaginator-only internals — self.key, self.max_limit, self._is_asc, self.build_queryset, self.count_hits, self.post_query_filter — none of which BasePaginator (whose own get_result at line ~815 takes only limit/cursor and returns CursorResult without hits/post_query_filter machinery) defines. The first paginated request through the new branch raises AttributeError (e.g. 'BasePaginator' object has no attribute 'max_limit'); even if attributes resolved, get_item_key applies math.floor/math.ceil directly to the raw 'datetime' attribute, raising TypeError on audit-log rows since no DateTimePaginator-style datetime-to-timestamp conversion exists.

[ADVISORY] The rewritten slicing in the shared get_result changes behavior for every existing paginator on this path: non-prev cursors with a negative offset previously crashed with AssertionError and now silently clamp to offset 0, returning first-page rows for a malformed cursor, while prev cursors with negative offsets still hit the negative-slice AssertionError. Clients (or proxies) that mangle cursor offsets get silently wrong data on every paginated list endpoint using this paginator class instead of a 4xx, and this shared-path behavior change ships with no test in the diff exercising it.

[ADVISORY] All new behavior-bearing logic in this diff — the OptimizedCursorPaginator class, the enable_advanced_features/negative-offset branch, and the endpoint's optimized_pagination gate — ships with zero test coverage; the diff contains no test-shaped files (no spec/**, test/**, *.test.* additions), so there is no verification of cursor correctness (next/prev round-trip, boundary trimming at lines 888-892) for the new class. Any regression in the new paginator's cursor arithmetic (e.g. the prev-trim condition `len(results) == offset + limit + extra` misbehaving with negative offsets) ships silently to production; a future refactor of the shared get_result has no test to detect the break.

[ADVISORY] The diff's stated acceptance criterion — 'Performance optimization for high-volume audit logs' — is not delivered by any mechanism: OptimizedCursorPaginator builds and slices the queryset identically to the existing path (same build_queryset, same list(queryset[start_offset:stop]) slice), and the only behavioral delta (negative offsets) does not change query cost, with no benchmark or measurement anywhere in the diff. The PR title's requirement is silently dropped: reviewers and operators accept a change that adds a crash-prone code path and admin gating while providing zero of the claimed performance benefit for high-volume audit log access.

[ADVISORY] The negative-offset 'feature' has no producer anywhere in the diff: build_cursor always emits cursors with offset >= 0, no client-side or documented contract exists for obtaining a negative-offset cursor, and no API surface generates one — the branch is reachable only via hand-crafted cursor strings. The ships-inert advanced-pagination feature cannot be exercised as designed by any real client; the only inputs that reach it are malformed cursors, which crash per the negative-slice defect, so the code exists purely as dead-plus-dangerous surface.

[ADVISORY] A new raw query parameter `optimized_pagination` gates a changed serialization/pagination path on a public API endpoint with no feature-flag or options entry, no documentation of the parameter, and no way to audit or globally disable it without a code deploy. The API's public surface silently grows: any user can probe the parameter, ops cannot turn the experimental path off during an incident without shipping code, and there is no flag under which the new behavior can be rollout-controlled or A/B verified.

[BUG] The negative-offset branch slices the queryset with a negative start (`start_offset = cursor.offset` then `queryset[start_offset:stop]`), but Django QuerySets raise `AssertionError: Negative indexing is not supported` on negative slice bounds, so the inline claim that 'the underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' is false. Any superuser or global-access member who sends `optimized_pagination=true` together with a cursor carrying a negative offset gets a 500 from the audit-logs endpoint instead of paginated results; the branch is unreachable-by-design dead code that can only produce an error, and it was added as 'advanced pagination' with no requirement asking for it.

[BUG] OptimizedCursorPaginator extends BasePaginator but its `get_result` calls `self.build_queryset(...)` and its `get_item_key` calls `self._is_asc(...)`, members that live on CursorPaginator, not BasePaginator; additionally `get_item_key` applies `math.floor(value)`/`math.ceil(value)` directly to `getattr(item, self.key)`, which for this endpoint's `order_by="-datetime"` is a datetime object, and `math.floor`/`math.ceil` on a datetime raises TypeError. The first request that actually reaches the optimized path (admin + `optimized_pagination=true`) raises AttributeError/TypeError inside the paginator and returns a 500; the class has never been executable as wired, confirming the new paginator is untraceable, unexercised surface rather than a working feature.

[ADVISORY] New endpoint behavior is gated on a raw, undocumented GET parameter (`request.GET.get("optimized_pagination") == "true"`) combined with an inline privilege check, with no feature flag or options entry anywhere in the diff. Operators cannot disable or roll back the new code path without a code deploy (rolling-deploy skew with no kill switch), out-of-tree API consumers see a silently changed public contract, and the comment's safety claim ('permissions are checked at the queryset level') is untested and only holds when the privilege check and paginator cooperate exactly as written.

[ADVISORY] The `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` change sits inside BasePaginator.get_result, the shared pagination path used by every cursor-paginated endpoint in the product, and no requirement in a PR titled 'audit log pagination performance' calls for changing it. Behavior of all other paginated endpoints changes silently as a side effect of an audit-log PR (any non-prev cursor with a previously crashing negative offset now clamps instead), so the next pagination bug report or regression will surface in an unrelated endpoint while the diff that caused it is attributed to audit logs; the raw client-supplied offset in the `is_prev` branch remains unclamped and untouched.

[ADVISORY] OptimizedCursorPaginator delivers no optimization: its else-branch executes the identical queryset slice as the existing paginator path, and the only functional delta (the negative-offset branch) crashes, so the PR's stated intent — performance for high-volume audit logs — is not implemented at all. The stated victims of the problem (high-volume audit log consumers) get nothing: the optimized path is additionally restricted to superusers/global-access members via an inline check, excluding exactly the machine accounts and integrations that generate high volume, while the codebase carries ~100 lines of new, broken, untraceable paginator surface to maintain.

[ADVISORY] The offset/extra/results slicing logic now exists in three hand-maintained copies in this file (BasePaginator.get_result, the OptimizedCursorPaginator else-branch, and the negative-offset branch), and drift between them is already observable in this diff: the base copy gained a `max(0, offset)` clamp while the `is_prev` handling differs between copies. The next change to pagination semantics (e.g., a real fix to prev-cursor boundary handling) must be found and replicated in three places; missing one produces paginators that disagree on cursor semantics for the same endpoint, and the deletion test is satisfied — collapsing to a single implementation makes the entire negative-offset branch and its 'advanced features' flag unnecessary.

[ADVISORY] The diff adds a new paginator class, a negative-offset execution branch, and a privilege-gated endpoint path with zero tests anywhere in the diff, and the mechanical evidence (the branch's false safety comment and the missing-member call pattern) shows the code has never been run. A regression in the negative-offset branch or the admin gating produces a 500 only for superusers/global-access members hitting an undocumented parameter — the exact population least likely to be covered by existing integration tests — and nothing in CI would catch it before users do.

[BUG] OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key calls math.floor/math.ceil directly on getattr(item, self.key), and the audit-log endpoint paginates on key 'datetime' (order_by="-datetime"), so every optimized-path request raises TypeError when building a cursor from a result row. The audit endpoint's optimized branch 500s on its very first page (build_cursor invokes get_item_key on the last result even when no cursor was supplied): math.floor() on a datetime.datetime raises "type datetime.datetime doesn't define __floor__ method". Unlike DateTimePaginator, which converts via value.timestamp(), this class subclasses BasePaginator directly and inherits no datetime handling, so the feature is dead on arrival for the only endpoint that uses it.

[BUG] The negative-offset branch slices the ORM queryset with a negative start (queryset[cursor.offset:stop]), which Django's QuerySet.__getitem__ rejects with ValueError("Negative indexing is not supported."), contradicting the comment's claim that the ORM handles negative slicing. Any superuser/global-access user who navigates with a cursor string carrying a negative offset (Cursor parsing accepts int("-5"), and cursors.py now invites exactly that) gets a 500 instead of a page. Even if Django permitted it, a negative OFFSET slice is not keyset pagination — it is a full-table scan — so the 'performance optimization' would be the opposite of its stated goal. The premise of the entire advanced feature is factually wrong about the data layer.

[BUG] enable_advanced is evaluated unconditionally on every request and references `organization_context`, which is not defined anywhere in the visible get() body or introduced by this diff, so any non-superuser request raises NameError before the use_optimized check short-circuits. For every non-superuser caller of the audit-log list endpoint (the normal case), the `or` chain evaluates organization_context.member.has_global_access and raises NameError -> 500, breaking the existing DateTimePaginator path too. Even if a name were intended from some enclosing scope, gating a pure pagination implementation choice behind member role is an ownership mistake: the queryset is already organization-scoped, so the gate adds a second, role-dependent code path for the same resource with no protective value.

[ADVISORY] OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result is a ~60-line verbatim copy of BasePaginator.get_result whose only behavioral delta is the broken negative-offset branch, duplicating the hits/max_hits/build_cursor/post_query_filter logic that base already owns. Every future fix to BasePaginator.get_result (hits accounting, prev-cursor edge cases, max_hits clamping) must now be mirrored here or the two paginators silently diverge — exactly the drift this copy already exhibits via get_item_key. The deletion test passes cleanly: removing the class and the endpoint branch eliminates both crash sites and the duplication, returning the endpoint to the existing DateTimePaginator path that already works.

[ADVISORY] The change to the shared BasePaginator.get_result hot path is behaviorally inert (max(0, offset) is a no-op for all reachable non-prev offsets) but is justified by a comment asserting Django 'will handle boundary conditions' for negative slicing, which is false. This code executes for every paginated endpoint in Sentry; churn here buys nothing while teaching future readers a false ORM fact. A later editor who 'removes the redundant clamp' per the comment's premise converts a working paginator into the same ValueError crash as the optimized branch. The edit should be reverted, not kept.

[ADVISORY] The added Cursor comments claim the change 'allows negative offsets' for 'efficient reverse pagination', but no behavior was added — int(offset) always accepted negatives and nothing downstream consumes them — so the comments document a capability that does not exist. The comment is the provenance statement legitimizing the negative-offset feature across two files; the next editor reading it has no signal that the entire mechanism is unsound, and may build additional negative-offset paths on a Cursor contract the ORM layer cannot honor. Comments that assert nonexistent behavior on a shared utility are worse than no comment.

[ADVISORY] The feature adds a second paginator selection branch to a stable endpoint whose only functional delta (negative offsets, uncoerced key math) is broken on both counts, delivering no working performance improvement over the existing DateTimePaginator cursor path. Operators get an admin-only 'optimized_pagination' flag whose activation strictly degrades behavior (500s), while maintainers inherit a parallel service path to test and keep in sync. The correct architectural move is to delete the OptimizedCursorPaginator class, the endpoint branch, and the cursors.py comments entirely; if large-dataset audit browsing is genuinely needed, it belongs in DateTimePaginator as a tested improvement, not a role-gated fork.

[BUG] The 'advanced feature' negative-offset branch slices the queryset with a negative start (results = list(queryset[start_offset:stop]) where start_offset = cursor.offset < 0), which Django's QuerySet.__getitem__ rejects with ValueError('Negative indexing is not supported.') — the in-code claim that 'the underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically' is false, so the stated intent of a 'safe' optimization is not what the code does. Any superuser or global-access member who requests optimized_pagination with a negative-offset cursor gets an unhandled ValueError → 500 response instead of a paginated result; the entire negative-offset capability the PR was iterated toward delivers a crash, not performance.

[ADVISORY] The PR's accepted objective (pagination performance for high-volume audit logs) was silently replaced during iteration by a different objective: a privilege-gated data-access mode — the new paginator's query path is algorithmically identical to the existing one (same build_queryset, same slicing math), so no performance improvement is delivered; the only functional delta is granting superusers/global-access members traversal 'beyond normal pagination bounds' via a raw query parameter. Reviewers and operators accept a 'performance optimization' and get an expanded access-semantics feature instead; the change of objective (performance → new admin navigation capability touching authorization-adjacent behavior) never received explicit human acceptance, and any incident triage will start from the wrong mental model of what this code does.

[ADVISORY] The shared paginator's get_result was modified under this audit-log PR, changing fleet-wide behavior beyond the accepted intent: previously a non-prev cursor with a negative offset crashed on the queryset slice (ValueError → 500); now max(0, offset) silently clamps it to page 0, so every endpoint using this paginator class (not just audit logs) silently changes failure behavior from error to data-returned. All endpoints using this paginator class change behavior in production under a PR scoped as 'audit log pagination'; clients that surfaced errors on malformed/negative cursors now silently receive first-page data, and this cross-cutting semantic change was not part of the objective anyone signed off on.

[ADVISORY] enable_advanced_features=True is hardcoded at the only call site, making the constructor flag a dead switch: the trio of gates (raw query param use_optimized, permission check enable_advanced, hardcoded enable_advanced_features) collapses to two, and the flag exists only to route into the crash-inducing negative-offset branch. Future readers must reason about three independently named switches where one is inert; deleting the enable_advanced_features parameter and the negative-offset branch leaves OptimizedCursorPaginator behaviorally identical to the base paginator, so the entire class (and the endpoint branch) becomes a pure deletion opportunity rather than a maintained duplicate.

[ADVISORY] OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result is a full copy-paste of the base paginator's get_result, and the copy has already drifted: the is_prev trim check compares len(results) == offset + limit + extra using the raw offset while the negative-offset branch sliced with start_offset, so the two variables no longer agree in the branch the copy exists to serve. The next change to pagination semantics must now be applied in two hand-maintained copies of ~70 lines; the observed offset/start_offset drift in this very diff demonstrates the copies diverge immediately, and any future fix to the base paginator silently misses the optimized copy.

[ADVISORY] The new pagination engine is gated on a raw query parameter (optimized_pagination=true) with no options entry or feature flag, so the behavior change cannot be disabled without a code deploy. If the optimized path misbehaves in production (e.g., the negative-offset 500 above), operators cannot turn it off via feature-flag tooling; mitigation requires an emergency deploy, and the per-request query-param switch means the two pagination engines for the same endpoint coexist with no centralized kill switch.

[BUG] The negative-offset branch slices the queryset with a user-controlled negative offset (request.cursor parses into Cursor.offset), which Django's QuerySet rejects, so the request dies with an unhandled AssertionError instead of a 4xx. An org admin (has_global_access) or superuser who sends optimized_pagination=true with a cursor containing a negative offset (e.g. '-1:5:0', cursors are unsigned/unvalidated) reaches queryset[-N:M]; Django's QuerySet.__getitem__ raises AssertionError('Negative indexing is not supported'), returning a 500 on every request with that cursor — the 'efficient bidirectional pagination' feature cannot work at all, and the inline safety rationale ('the underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically') is false, so the code path ships enabled for admins with no working behavior and no way to serve a graceful error.

[ADVISORY] The admin-only optimized pagination code path is gated solely on the raw client-supplied query parameter optimized_pagination with no feature flag or options entry, so this behavior-altering switch cannot be disabled without a code deploy. Operators bitten during incident response: once this ships, any admin client sending optimized_pagination=true selects the new paginator (including the crashing negative-offset path above); if it misbehaves in production there is no settings/flag kill-switch — remediation requires rolling back the deploy, and the security-relevant branch selection is driven by an unvalidated GET parameter rather than server-controlled configuration.

[BUG] The advanced negative-offset branch slices the Django queryset with a negative start index, which Django's QuerySet.__getitem__ rejects with AssertionError ('Negative indexing is not supported'), so the advertised 'efficient reverse pagination' feature crashes with a 500 on any request whose cursor carries a negative offset (client-controlled via the cursor query param, e.g. cursor=1:-5:0). A superuser/global-access admin using optimized_pagination with a negative-offset cursor gets an unhandled AssertionError surfacing as a 500 instead of the 4xx the API contract promises for malformed cursors; the headline feature of this diff cannot execute its advanced path even once. The in-code justification ('the underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically') is factually false, so the crash is guaranteed, not conditional.

[BUG] OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key applies math.floor/math.ceil directly to the raw attribute value, but the endpoint uses it with order_by='-datetime', so on the first non-empty page build_cursor raises TypeError ('datetime.datetime' object cannot be interpreted as an integer) — or AttributeError on self.key if BasePaginator never sets key from order_by, since the endpoint passes only order_by and no key. Every optimized-pagination request that returns at least one audit-log row fails with an unhandled exception (500); the optimized path is dead on arrival and every invocation by an admin produces a 500 rather than paginated results. The floor/ceil implementation only works for numeric key values (it is a copy of the numeric-key Paginator.get_item_key), while this endpoint's key is a datetime.

[BUG] The rewritten base get_result clamps negative offsets only for non-prev cursors (max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev), so an is_prev cursor with a negative offset — client-supplied via the cursor query string — still evaluates queryset[-N:stop], which Django rejects with AssertionError, producing a 500 instead of a 4xx on the default (non-optimized) audit-log path. Any caller (not just admins) who sends a prev cursor with a negative offset gets an unhandled 500; the diff rewrote exactly this expression and added a comment claiming 'the underlying queryset will handle boundary conditions', yet the is_prev branch retains the crash. The clamp added for the non-prev case silently changes those requests to serve offset-0 data with a 200 and no signal that the requested position was invalid.

[ADVISORY] OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result duplicates ~50 lines of the base get_result verbatim instead of subclassing and hooking the offset computation, and the copy has already drifted from the code it was copied from: the prev-trim comparison uses 'offset + limit + extra' while the slice uses start_offset, and the base's negative-offset clamp differs between the two copies. The next fix to cursor/boundary logic in the base paginator (e.g. a real fix for the negative-offset AssertionError) will not propagate to this copy, leaving the optimized path silently behaving differently from the default path on the same endpoint; the two get_result bodies must now be hand-synced on every paginator change. Subclassing with a single overridable offset-computation hook would delete the entire duplicated block and its divergent branches.

If `BasePaginator` is not already defined earlier in this module, the class statement will raise `NameError` at import time and break imports of `sentry.api.paginator`. This newly introduced free variable would raise `NameError` when that line executes (i.e., when the endpoint is hit), making the `optimized_pagination=true` path potentially unreachable.

Whether this is a real pagination correctness bug (cursor value not applied, repeated first page) depends entirely on what `BasePaginator.build_queryset` does, which is not shown in the diff. The finding highlights a concrete, diff-grounded risk/contract mismatch, but the claimed broken behavior cannot be verified from the provided changes alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The shared paginator's get_result was modified under this audit-log PR, changing fleet-wide behavior beyond the accepted intent: previously a non-prev cursor with a negative offset crashed on the queryset slice (ValueError → 500); now max(0, offset) silently clamps it to page 0, so every endpoint using this paginator class (not just audit logs) silently changes failure behavior from error to data-returned. All endpoints using this paginator class change behavior in production under a PR scoped as 'audit log pagination'; clients that surfaced errors on malformed/negative cursors now silently receive first-page data, and this cross-cutting semantic change was not part of the objective anyone signed off on.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows a fleet-wide behavior change in the shared paginator: in `src/sentry/api/paginator.py` the slice start is changed from `queryset[offset:stop]` to `queryset[start_offset:stop]` where `start_offset = max(0, offset)` for non-`prev` cursors. This means negative `cursor.offset` values are now silently clamped to 0 (returning first-page data) instead of being passed through to the ORM slice. Regardless of whether the prior behavior raised, this is a cross-cutting semantic change affecting all endpoints using this paginator, and it’s introduced in an audit-log-scoped PR, matching the finding’s scope/intent concern.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] enable_advanced_features=True is hardcoded at the only call site, making the constructor flag a dead switch: the trio of gates (raw query param use_optimized, permission check enable_advanced, hardcoded enable_advanced_features) collapses to two, and the flag exists only to route into the crash-inducing negative-offset branch. Future readers must reason about three independently named switches where one is inert; deleting the enable_advanced_features parameter and the negative-offset branch leaves OptimizedCursorPaginator behaviorally identical to the base paginator, so the entire class (and the endpoint branch) becomes a pure deletion opportunity rather than a maintained duplicate.

adjudication.rationale: In the new endpoint branch, `OptimizedCursorPaginator` is only instantiated via `self.paginate(... paginator_cls=OptimizedCursorPaginator, enable_advanced_features=True ...)`, i.e. the new constructor flag is always forced on at the only visible call site in this diff. That makes the extra `enable_advanced_features` switch redundant within the shown changes (the real gating is already `optimized_pagination` + `enable_advanced`). This is a concrete maintainability/complexity issue introduced by the diff (multiple independently named gates where one is effectively inert here), rather than a directly proven functional defect from the diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result is a full copy-paste of the base paginator's get_result, and the copy has already drifted: the is_prev trim check compares len(results) == offset + limit + extra using the raw offset while the negative-offset branch sliced with start_offset, so the two variables no longer agree in the branch the copy exists to serve. The next change to pagination semantics must now be applied in two hand-maintained copies of ~70 lines; the observed offset/start_offset drift in this very diff demonstrates the copies diverge immediately, and any future fix to the base paginator silently misses the optimized copy.

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces a new `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result` implementation that substantially duplicates the existing pagination logic (cursor setup, hits counting, offset/extra handling, slicing, prev-trimming, reversing, cursor building, post-filtering). This creates real maintenance/architecture risk: future fixes/semantics changes to the existing paginator logic will need to be duplicated here as well. However, the specific “offset/start_offset drift causes incorrect `len(results) == offset + limit + extra` behavior” is not clearly verifiable from this diff because that trim check only runs under `if cursor.is_prev and cursor.value`, and in both branches shown `start_offset` equals `offset` when `cursor.is_prev` is true. So the duplication concern is grounded, but the claimed concrete bug from drift is not demonstrated by the shown code.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The new pagination engine is gated on a raw query parameter (optimized_pagination=true) with no options entry or feature flag, so the behavior change cannot be disabled without a code deploy. If the optimized path misbehaves in production (e.g., the negative-offset 500 above), operators cannot turn it off via feature-flag tooling; mitigation requires an emergency deploy, and the per-request query-param switch means the two pagination engines for the same endpoint coexist with no centralized kill switch.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows the new paginator path is enabled purely via a per-request raw query param: `use_optimized = request.GET.get("optimized_pagination") == "true"`, combined with an admin check, and there is no feature flag/config option in the shown code to centrally disable it. This means both pagination engines can coexist for the same endpoint depending on request parameters, and there’s no kill switch evident in the diff beyond clients not sending the param.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The negative-offset branch slices the queryset with a user-controlled negative offset (request.cursor parses into Cursor.offset), which Django's QuerySet rejects, so the request dies with an unhandled AssertionError instead of a 4xx. An org admin (has_global_access) or superuser who sends optimized_pagination=true with a cursor containing a negative offset (e.g. '-1:5:0', cursors are unsigned/unvalidated) reaches queryset[-N:M]; Django's QuerySet.__getitem__ raises AssertionError('Negative indexing is not supported'), returning a 500 on every request with that cursor — the 'efficient bidirectional pagination' feature cannot work at all, and the inline safety rationale ('the underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically') is false, so the code path ships enabled for admins with no working behavior and no way to serve a graceful error.

adjudication.rationale: The diff introduces a code path that slices a Django QuerySet with a negative start index. In `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result`, when `enable_advanced_features` is true and `cursor.offset < 0`, it sets `start_offset = cursor.offset` and executes `queryset[start_offset:stop]`. Django QuerySet slicing does not support negative indexing and typically raises an `AssertionError` for negative offsets, which would surface as a 500 if not caught. The endpoint enables this paginator for `optimized_pagination=true` when the user is a superuser or has `has_global_access`, making the failing behavior reachable. The inline comment claiming Django ORM “properly handles negative slicing automatically” is contradicted by Django’s known behavior and the absence of any validation/exception handling in the diff.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] The admin-only optimized pagination code path is gated solely on the raw client-supplied query parameter optimized_pagination with no feature flag or options entry, so this behavior-altering switch cannot be disabled without a code deploy. Operators bitten during incident response: once this ships, any admin client sending optimized_pagination=true selects the new paginator (including the crashing negative-offset path above); if it misbehaves in production there is no settings/flag kill-switch — remediation requires rolling back the deploy, and the security-relevant branch selection is driven by an unvalidated GET parameter rather than server-controlled configuration.

adjudication.rationale: In `organization_auditlogs.py`, the new paginator selection is controlled by the raw query parameter `optimized_pagination` (`use_optimized = request.GET.get("optimized_pagination") == "true"`) plus an admin check, with no server-controlled feature flag or setting shown in the diff. That means once deployed, any qualifying admin client can opt into the new behavior and operators have no runtime kill-switch in this code path. The finding’s core point is therefore diff-grounded, but it’s primarily an operational/rollout concern rather than a concrete correctness defect proven by the diff alone.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The advanced negative-offset branch slices the Django queryset with a negative start index, which Django's QuerySet.__getitem__ rejects with AssertionError ('Negative indexing is not supported'), so the advertised 'efficient reverse pagination' feature crashes with a 500 on any request whose cursor carries a negative offset (client-controlled via the cursor query param, e.g. cursor=1:-5:0). A superuser/global-access admin using optimized_pagination with a negative-offset cursor gets an unhandled AssertionError surfacing as a 500 instead of the 4xx the API contract promises for malformed cursors; the headline feature of this diff cannot execute its advanced path even once. The in-code justification ('the underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically') is factually false, so the crash is guaranteed, not conditional.

adjudication.rationale: In `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result`, the "advanced" branch explicitly allows `start_offset = cursor.offset` when `cursor.offset < 0` and then slices the queryset as `queryset[start_offset:stop]` (negative start index). The diff also removes any guarding of negative offsets in `Cursor` (it just `int(offset)`), so a client-controlled cursor can carry a negative offset and reach this code path when `optimized_pagination=true` and `enable_advanced_features` is set. Given Django QuerySet slicing semantics, negative indexing is not supported and will raise, causing a 500 rather than a controlled 4xx for malformed cursors; the code comment claiming ORM handles negative slicing contradicts this.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key applies math.floor/math.ceil directly to the raw attribute value, but the endpoint uses it with order_by='-datetime', so on the first non-empty page build_cursor raises TypeError ('datetime.datetime' object cannot be interpreted as an integer) — or AttributeError on self.key if BasePaginator never sets key from order_by, since the endpoint passes only order_by and no key. Every optimized-pagination request that returns at least one audit-log row fails with an unhandled exception (500); the optimized path is dead on arrival and every invocation by an admin produces a 500 rather than paginated results. The floor/ceil implementation only works for numeric key values (it is a copy of the numeric-key Paginator.get_item_key), while this endpoint's key is a datetime.

adjudication.rationale: In the new optimized path, `organization_auditlogs.get()` calls `self.paginate(... paginator_cls=OptimizedCursorPaginator, order_by="-datetime" ...)`. `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_item_key()` does `value = getattr(item, self.key)` and then applies `math.floor/math.ceil` and `int(...)` to that value. For audit log rows, the `datetime` field is a `datetime.datetime`, so `math.floor(datetime_obj)` (and `int(...)`) will raise `TypeError`. Additionally, the endpoint provides `order_by` but no explicit `key`, so if `BasePaginator` does not set `self.key` from `order_by`, `getattr(item, self.key)` could also fail; either way the optimized pagination path is broken for non-empty result sets.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [BUG] The rewritten base get_result clamps negative offsets only for non-prev cursors (max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev), so an is_prev cursor with a negative offset — client-supplied via the cursor query string — still evaluates queryset[-N:stop], which Django rejects with AssertionError, producing a 500 instead of a 4xx on the default (non-optimized) audit-log path. Any caller (not just admins) who sends a prev cursor with a negative offset gets an unhandled 500; the diff rewrote exactly this expression and added a comment claiming 'the underlying queryset will handle boundary conditions', yet the is_prev branch retains the crash. The clamp added for the non-prev case silently changes those requests to serve offset-0 data with a 200 and no signal that the requested position was invalid.

adjudication.rationale: In src/sentry/api/paginator.py the rewritten BasePaginator.get_result computes `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset`, so when `cursor.is_prev` is true a client-supplied negative `cursor.offset` will be used directly in `queryset[start_offset:stop]`. Django QuerySet slicing rejects negative indices (raises AssertionError), and the diff shows no validation/handling around this, so it can result in an unhandled 500 on the non-optimized path. The accompanying comment in utils/cursors.py also indicates offsets are now allowed to be negative, increasing exposure.

adjudication_records.issue_text: [ADVISORY] OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result duplicates ~50 lines of the base get_result verbatim instead of subclassing and hooking the offset computation, and the copy has already drifted from the code it was copied from: the prev-trim comparison uses 'offset + limit + extra' while the slice uses start_offset, and the base's negative-offset clamp differs between the two copies. The next fix to cursor/boundary logic in the base paginator (e.g. a real fix for the negative-offset AssertionError) will not propagate to this copy, leaving the optimized path silently behaving differently from the default path on the same endpoint; the two get_result bodies must now be hand-synced on every paginator change. Subclassing with a single overridable offset-computation hook would delete the entire duplicated block and its divergent branches.

adjudication.rationale: The diff adds a new `OptimizedCursorPaginator.get_result` that largely re-implements cursor pagination logic instead of reusing/extending an existing paginator method. This is verifiable in `src/sentry/api/paginator.py`, where the new class duplicates substantial logic (cursor setup, hit counting, queryset build, slicing, prev-trim, reversing, cursor building) with its own branches (e.g. `enable_advanced_features` negative-offset path). This creates a real maintainability/architecture risk: future fixes to boundary/offset/cursor logic in the existing paginator code (also modified in this PR around `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset`) will not automatically apply to the optimized path, and the two can silently diverge. The finding’s point about drift/hand-syncing is grounded in the duplicated bodies, even if the specific mismatch it cites may not currently surface as an obvious runtime defect from the shown code alone.
